title: Elie Wiesel
wiki_lead:
Eliezer "Elie" Wiesel (September 30, 1928 – July 2, 2016) was a Romanian-born American writer, professor, political activist, Nobel laureate, and Holocaust survivor. He authored 57 books, written mostly in French and English, including Night, which is based on his experiences as a Jewish prisoner at Auschwitz and Buchenwald during the Holocaust.
As a political activist, Wiesel became a regular speaker on the subject of the Holocaust and advocated for justice in numerous causes around the globe, including that of Soviet Jews and Ethiopian Jews, South African apartheid, the Rwandan genocide, the Bosnian genocide, the War in Darfur, the Kurdish independence movement, the Armenian genocide, Argentina's Desaparecidos, Nicaragua's Miskito people, the Sri Lankan Tamils, and the Cambodian genocide. He was also an outspoken advocate for Israel and frequently weighed in to support the country during escalations of the Arab–Israeli conflict and throughout the Iran–Israel proxy conflict. He backed Netanyahu publicly, including his controversial 2015 Congress speech on Iran, and signed ads praising Jewish settlers. He said Jerusalem "belongs to the Jewish people" and opposed territorial compromise there. He also hosted direct talks to facilitate the Israeli–Palestinian peace process.
Wiesel was a professor of the humanities at Boston University, which created the Elie Wiesel Center for Jewish Studies in his honor. He received a number of awards, including the Nobel Peace Prize in 1986. He was a founding board member of the Human Rights Foundation and remained active in it throughout his life. Wiesel was one of the main figures who spearheaded the establishment of the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in 1993.

Early life and education

Eliezer Wiesel was born in Sighet (now Sighetu Marmației), Maramureș, in the Carpathian Mountains of Romania. His parents were Sarah Feig and Shlomo Wiesel. At home, the family spoke mainly Yiddish in addition to German, Hungarian, and Romanian. Wiesel's mother, Sarah, was the daughter of Dodye Feig, a Vizhnitz Hasid and farmer from the nearby village of Bocskó. Dodye was active and trusted within the community. 
Wiesel's father, Shlomo, instilled a strong sense of humanism in his son, encouraging him to learn Hebrew and to read literature, whereas his mother encouraged him to study the Torah. Wiesel said his father represented reason, while his mother Sarah promoted faith. Wiesel was instructed that his genealogy traced back to Rabbi Schlomo Yitzhaki (Rashi), and was a descendant of Rabbi Yeshayahu ben Abraham Horovitz ha-Levi.
Wiesel had three siblings. His older sisters were Beatrice and Hilda, and a younger sister Tzipora. Beatrice and Hilda survived the war, and were reunited with Wiesel at a French orphanage. They eventually emigrated to North America, with Beatrice moving to Montreal, Quebec, Canada. Tzipora, Shlomo, and Sarah were murdered in the Holocaust.
As Wiesel himself stated, his family was Hungarian-speaking and felt little connection to the Kingdom of Romania. As such, they supported the Second Vienna Award, which awarded Northern Transylvania - including Sighet - to the Kingdom of Hungary, despite the fact that Hungary implemented its own antisemitic legislation. Elie Wiesel declared that his mother, Sarah, welcomed the Hungarian occupying troops in Sighet, with her stating that that being under Hungarian rule reminds her of her happy childhood.


Imprisonment during the Holocaust

In March 1944, Germany occupied Hungary, thus extending the Holocaust into Northern Transylvania as well. Wiesel was 15, and he, with his family, along with the rest of the town's Jewish population, was placed in one of the two confinement ghettos set up in Máramarossziget (Sighet), the town where he had been born and raised. grok_lead: Elie Wiesel (September 30, 1928 â July 2, 2016) was a Romanian-born American author, academic, and advocate whose memoir Night detailed his survival of Nazi concentration camps during the Holocaust. Born in Sighet, Transylvania (then part of Romania), Wiesel was deported with his family to Auschwitz-Birkenau in 1944 at age 15; his mother and younger sister perished there, while he and his father were transferred to Buchenwald, where his father died shortly before liberation by American forces in April 1945. After the war, Wiesel studied at the Sorbonne in Paris, worked as a journalist for Yiddish publications, and immigrated to the United States in 1956, becoming a citizen in 1963. His seminal work Night, originally published in French as La Nuit in 1958 and in English in 1960, drew from a longer Yiddish manuscript ( Un di velt hot geshvign, 1956) but condensed and revised its content, shifting from raw expressions of Jewish rage against the world to a more restrained testimony focused on the camps' horrors. The book gained widespread acclaim, selling millions after endorsements like Oprah Winfrey's book club selection in 2006, though some critics have noted its blend of factual recollection with literary shaping, including timeline compressions and emotional emphases not strictly matching historical records. Wiesel authored over 50 books, taught Jewish studies and humanities at Boston University from 1976 to 2013, and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1986 for alerting the world to the dangers of indifference to human suffering, particularly through his testimony on the Holocaust and advocacy against racism, apartheid, and genocide. He founded the Elie Wiesel Foundation for Humanity in 1987 to promote ethical discussions on global issues and support humanitarian causes. His activism extended to fervent support for Israel and Soviet Jewry, but drew controversy for selective emphases, such as initial reluctance on non-Jewish genocides and 2014 full-page advertisements condemning Hamas's use of children as human shields (comparing the tactics to child sacrifice and Nazis), which some fellow Holocaust survivors rebuked as an abuse of history. Posthumously, a woman claimed Wiesel groped her at a 1989 charity event when she was 19; the allegation was unproven and denied by his foundation and associates. Despite such scrutiny, Wiesel's influence shaped public understanding of the Holocaust, emphasizing remembrance as a bulwark against recurrence, while critiques highlight how his narrative sometimes prioritized moral symbolism over unvarnished historical causality.
